clue.text: Ted to Maggie? A right cold weed with hint of femininity inside

definitions.note: Edward Heath was famously hostile to Margaret Thatcher, who ousted him as Tory leader

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the femininity letter sits within the weeding word

parts.note: to hoe is to weed a bed, so the verb gives the garden tool's name

indicators.note: a hint is just a trace, so only the opening letter of femininity is used

parts.note: only the first letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A satirical aside about Ted Heath and Maggie Thatcher, dressed up as a description of some feminised garden weed.
explanation.walkthrough: Ted is Edward Heath, Conservative prime minister before Margaret Thatcher deposed him; the question mark marks the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Heath remained Thatcher's bitterest opponent within her own party, a principal enemy in every sense.

clue.text: Let-down Northern relative cried out with orgasm

indicators.note: spoken aloud, the relative's pet name sounds like the prefix meaning against

parts.note: an aunt, called auntie, especially in Northern speech
a sexual climax

explanation.surface: A disappointing night: someone's northern auntie crying out at the moment of orgasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cried out' tempts a sexual reading, but it signals the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that fails to live up to the build-up before it is a disappointing flop.

clue.text: Phwoar! Females undo tops in this holiday spot

parts.note: cor is the British exclamation of surprise or lust

indicators.note: the tops of the two words are their opening letters

parts.note: only the opening letter of each word is used

explanation.surface: A leering cry as women go topless at a beach resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tops' reads as bikini tops coming undone, but it takes the opening letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek island in the Ionian Sea is a popular package-holiday destination.

clue.text: Area of influence demanding Falconer's head if Dome disastrous

indicators.note: the head of a name is its first letter

parts.note: Lord Falconer, only his initial is used

indicators.note: a disastrous project is a mess, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Lord Falconer's sphere of influence demands his head because the Millennium Dome was a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie Falconer was the minister responsible for the ill-fated Millennium Dome in London.
explanation.definitionFit: A fief was land held under a lord, and the word now means anyone's personal sphere of control.

clue.text: Neil 'Tit' Kinnock's heart broken by Glenys's first calling

indicators.note: a broken word has its letters smashed and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the heart is the central letter of the surname, ignoring the possessive

parts.note: the central letter of the surname, the possessive set aside

indicators.note: the first letter of the name is taken

parts.note: only the first letter of Glenys Kinnock's name

explanation.surface: Insulting Neil Kinnock as a tit, broken-hearted by his wife Glenys's vocation.
explanation.walkthrough: Neil Kinnock was Labour leader in the 1980s and Glenys his wife, also a politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a name is giving them a title, so the two verbs share the sense of naming.

clue.text: An element of extra advantage getting tossed by Ben

indicators.note: tossing the letters around jumbles their order

parts.note: a plus is a bonus or extra advantage
Ben-Hur, the epic film hero, so Ben suggests his surname

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of some advantage being tossed off by a man named Ben.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben-Hur is the chariot-racing hero of the Charlton Heston film; the clue relies on completing his name.
explanation.definitionFit: The yellow non-metal with symbol S is one of the chemical elements of the periodic table.

clue.text: 'Gold-hearted' doctors need rise, kid

definitions.note: sprog is British slang for a child

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the letters are read from the bottom up
the clue word that signals this step

parts.note: GPs are general practitioners, family doctors
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: Doctors with hearts of gold say a pay rise is needed, and they're not kidding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gold-hearted' says the gold word sits at the heart of the doctors; 'kid' looks like a verb but is the child. A sprog is British slang for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprog is informal British slang for a young child or baby, the same as a kid.

clue.text: Roger to get this, for example, in Beau's embrace

indicators.note: the lover's letters wrap around the abbreviation

parts.note: a beau is a boyfriend or lover

explanation.surface: Roger hoping for some action, held in a boyfriend's arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roger' reads as a man's name but is the British slang verb for having sex; to get one's leg over is the same.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang phrase for having sex is to get your leg over, so roger to get this exactly.

clue.text: Try to shag at a party

parts.note: to have someone is slang for having sex with them
taken as written
a bash is an informal party

explanation.surface: An attempt to pull and have sex at a party.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom means to make an attempt at something, to give it a go.

clue.text: Regulation markedly stiff length?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a principle or law that governs conduct
second meaning: a rigid measuring stick marked with units

explanation.walkthrough: The second half sounds like an innuendo but is a playful description of a measuring rod.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a principle laid down and a straight graduated measuring strip.

clue.text: Groups practising troilism, perhaps, with sailor (rating)

parts.note: troilism is sex among three people, so such groups are threes or threesomes
Jack Tar is the traditional nickname for a seaman

explanation.surface: Threesome enthusiasts joined by a sailor, with a bracketed rating for the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rating' looks like a naval rank for the sailor, but it is the definition: a mark of quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotels and restaurants are graded by stars, and a three-star grade is a middling quality mark.

clue.text: Used by judge to get quiet girl to hold very head of erection

definitions.text: Used by judge to get quiet

indicators.note: the girl word holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: gal is an informal word for a girl

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: only the first letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A judge silencing the court by having a girl grip the tip of an erection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erection' tempts a rude reading, but only its first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A judge or auctioneer bangs a small wooden mallet to call for order and silence.

clue.text: Was a useless wanker but didn't care

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: someone unable to masturbate successfully, as a hopeless wanker would be
second meaning: the idiom for being completely indifferent

explanation.walkthrough: 'Toss' is British slang both for masturbation and for the least amount of care, so the idiom reads two ways.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a common British idiom for total indifference, taken literally as a sexual failure.

clue.text: See 11
Diplomat, one who needs to get a life, loses day in endless Mars Bar abuse

indicators.note: abused letters are mistreated and knocked out of order
the day abbreviation is lost from the pathetic person

parts.words: one who needs to get a life
parts.note: a saddo is a pathetic person told to get a life

indicators.note: with no end, the chocolate bar's name drops its final letter

parts.note: the chocolate bar's name, taken as written before it is shortened

explanation.surface: A sad diplomat losing a day to some endless abuse involving a Mars bar.
explanation.walkthrough: A saddo is British slang for a pathetic loser; the Mars bar alludes to a notorious tabloid sex rumour.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior envoy representing his government abroad is the top rank of diplomat.

clue.text: One unable to get off with Simon turning to get back in with Bill

indicators.note: turning the letters over and around rearranges them

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
AC is short for account, which is a bill

explanation.surface: Someone who can't get off with a woman because Simon has come back to her with Bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get off' reads as sexual success but here means getting off to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A person suffering from chronic sleeplessness cannot drop off at night.

clue.text: Potentially lethal plant — needs stiffener and healthy nip of brandy

parts.note: size is a glue-like stiffening agent for paper and cloth
being well is being healthy

indicators.note: a nip is a small taste, so only the first letter

parts.note: only the first letter of the drink is used

explanation.surface: A dangerous plant that requires a stiffener, a tonic and a nip of brandy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' suggests a poisonous shrub, but means a power station; Sizewell B is a nuclear reactor in Suffolk.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuclear power station could cause lethal radiation if it failed, so plant is industrial.

clue.text: Head done in by company name: "Pain in the Arse"

parts.note: a cussed person is awkward and contrary, a pain in the arse

explanation.surface: A boss done in by a company called Pain in the Arse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' reads as a company boss, but it is the brain that gets hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: A blow that leaves the brain injured and the person dazed has done in their head.

clue.text: Flesh and blood male dominated by Brenda

definitions.note: Private Eye calls the Queen Brenda, and her kingdom is the territory she rules: a noun phrase for the thing she dominates

parts.note: something of flesh and blood is real rather than imaginary

explanation.surface: A real man kept firmly under the thumb of a woman called Brenda.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: A kingdom is the domain a monarch rules over, so it is what the Queen holds sway over.

clue.text: Vanessa's tip: "Zion activity here in Italy"

indicators.note: the tip here is the end of the name itself, setting aside the possessive

parts.note: the last letter of the name, the possessive set aside

indicators.note: activity sets the letters in motion so they rearrange

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Vanessa offers a tip about Zionist activity taking place somewhere in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: Vanessa suggests Vanessa Redgrave, known for anti-Zionist campaigning.
explanation.definitionFit: The coastal town south of Rome was the scene of the 1944 Allied landings, a place in Italy.

clue.text: Keep an eye on the sportsman's balls and churchman's seat

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled
a see is a bishop's seat or diocese

explanation.surface: Keeping an eye on a sportsman's balls and a bishop's chair.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket deliveries come in overs of six balls each.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversee something is to supervise it, watching over the work being done.

clue.text: Norah, ego ruffled, absorbs climax of thunder clap

indicators.note: the mixed letters take in the other letter
ruffled things are disordered, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: a climax is the end point, so the final letter is used

parts.note: only the final letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: Norah, ego dented, soaks up the climactic thunderclap of a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clap' looks like part of thunderclap but is slang for a venereal disease; this is the American spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The clap is long-standing slang for the sexually transmitted infection caused by gonococcus bacteria.

clue.text: Alien stunners tore top of shorts holding guy off

indicators.note: the running word holds the other letters

parts.note: tore as in sped along, the same as ran

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

parts.note: only the first letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: Gorgeous aliens ripping off a man's shorts with him inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stunners' reads as beautiful women but means weapons that stun.
explanation.definitionFit: Science-fiction aliens zap people with beam weapons that stun or kill.

clue.text: Wife has leg up for young upstart

parts.note: a leg up is a boost or bit of help

explanation.surface: A wife hitching her leg up in the presence of some cocky youngster.
explanation.definitionFit: A whelp is a puppy, and by extension an impudent, presumptuous youth.

clue.text: Bush and local El Salvador leaders

parts.note: a local is one's neighbourhood pub

indicators.note: the leaders of the two words are their first letters

parts.note: only the opening letter of each word is used

explanation.surface: George Bush and the local leaders of El Salvador meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' looks like the American president, but it is slang for pubic hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Bush is slang for a tuft of pubic hair, which is what the answer means.

clue.text: Increase what you have and get stuffed

parts.note: to up something is to increase it
what you own is yours

explanation.surface: Advice to boost your holdings, followed by a rude brush-off.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as an instruction it means raise your own stake; said as an exclamation it is a crude dismissal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are rude British exclamations of contemptuous rejection, telling someone to go away.

clue.text: Kissinger's other set of tits?

indicators.note: Henry Kissinger's thick German accent turned the word into something with a hard d

parts.note: said in Kissinger's accent this word comes out with the th as a d

explanation.surface: A schoolboy joke about Henry Kissinger's other pair of breasts.
explanation.walkthrough: Kissinger's heavy German accent is mimicked; the question mark warns that tits here are teats.
explanation.definitionFit: A cow's udder carries several teats, a set of tits in the farmyard sense.

clue.text: See 11
Looks like a lecher's sole perversion, grabbing Morag's bottom

indicators.note: the twisted letters grab hold of another letter inside them
perverting a word twists its letters out of order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the bottom of the name is its last letter, setting aside the possessive

parts.note: the last letter of the Scottish name, the possessive set aside

explanation.surface: A lecher whose one perversion is grabbing Morag's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sole' reads as only, but it is the four letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle is to stare at someone with obvious sexual desire, the lecher's typical leer.

clue.text: Sexually active type in his element with journalist wearing body jewellery

indicators.note: the stud goes inside the bed word

parts.note: a stud is most at home in bed, his natural element
a stud is a man with a lively sex life
ED is the usual crossword editor

explanation.surface: A randy type in his element with a pierced journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In his element' reads as an idiom for being comfortable, but it supplies the place a stud thrives.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorated all over with studs, the small metal pieces used in piercings, ears, tongues and navels.

clue.text: Makes an accommodating arrangement of Duff Street Blues

indicators.note: duff means faulty or useless, so the letters are botched into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone arranging a gig for a band called the Duff Street Blues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duff' looks like part of a band or street name, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenant who lets their rented home to someone else arranges accommodation for them.

clue.text: One who fancies O'Connor and Paddy King

parts.note: Des O'Connor was a British TV entertainer and singer
being in a paddy is being in a rage, so it means ire

explanation.surface: An admirer with a crush on both Des O'Connor and some Irish king.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddy reads as an Irish name, but it is the British slang for a temper tantrum.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who wants or craves another person is one who has a longing for them.
